'''Cryptography Research, Inc.''' was a [[San Francisco]] based cryptography company specializing in applied cryptographic engineering, including technologies for building tamper-resistant [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]].  It was purchased on June 6, 2011, by [[Rambus]] for $342.5M and remained active as a [[subsidiary]] until 2015.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/227797/rambus_buying_cryptography_research_for_3425_million.html | title=Rambus Buying Cryptography Research for $342.5 Million | date=2011-05-12 | accessdate=2012-06-16 | archive-date=2011-08-28 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110828001718/http://www.pcworld.com/article/227797/rambus_buying_cryptography_research_for_3425_million.html | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | date=n.d. | url=http://www.cryptography.com/ | title=Home page | publisher=Cryptography Research | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150824065654/http://www.cryptography.com/ | archivedate=August 24, 2015}} Compare with next available archived snapshot</ref>  The company licensed patents for protecting cryptographic devices against [[power analysis]] attacks.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.frost.com/prod/servlet/market-insight-top.pag?docid=28127384|last=Ubhey |first=Anoop |title=Interview with Cryptography Research Inc |publisher= Frost.com |date=November 23, 2004}}</ref> The company's CryptoFirewall-brand [[ASIC]] cores were used in pay [[TV]] [[conditional access]] systems and anti-counterfeiting applications.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.devicelink.com/mddi/archive/07/10/020.html |first=Maria |last=Fontanezza |title=Technology Battles Device Cloning - MD&DI |date=October 2007 |access-date=2008-07-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090207022010/http://www.devicelink.com/mddi/archive/07/10/020.html |archive-date=2009-02-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref> CRI also developed [[BD+]], a security component in the Blu-ray disc format, and played a role in the [[High-definition optical disc format war|format war]] between [[HD DVD]] and [[Blu-ray]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/04/15/business/technology-plan-would-use-content-not-devices-to-fight-piracy.html|last=Markoff |first= John |title=Plan Would Use Content, Not Devices, to Fight Piracy |work= The New York Times |date=15 April 2003}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://blog.wired.com/27bstroke6/2008/02/how-crypto-won.html|first=Ryan |last=Singel |title=How Crypto Won the DVD War |publisher= Wired Magazine |date=February 28, 2008|magazine=WIRED}}</ref>  The company's services group assisted with security testing, disaster recovery, and training.

Cryptography Research protected its core operations from outside attack by maintaining a secured local network that is not connected to the [[Internet]] at all. Employees who needed to work with sensitive data had two computers on their desks — one to access the secure network, and a separate computer to access the Internet.<ref>[http://news.cnet.com/8301-27080_3-20001391-245.html?tag=nl.e703 "How one company stays safe with two networks"], [[CNET News]], March 30, 2010.</ref>
